Thank you both for those critical disclosures. Let me make sure I understand the implications before I make my sign-off.

Leila, so we can only fund $9 million before the end of the current fiscal year while preserving the approved minimum cash floor, and the remaining $3 million must be funded after October 1. That's a real constraint we need to plan around.

Grant, the 20% holdback on each implementation invoice until final acceptance is significant. That means the vendor won't actually receive 20% of each invoice until we reach final acceptance — so the cash outflow timing shifts. This actually interacts directly with Leila's cash-flow concern: the holdback effectively defers a portion of the cash payments, which could help align our funding capacity with the payment schedule.

Let me think through this: on a $12 million budget with a 20% holdback, $2.4 million would be held back until final acceptance. That means only $9.6 million would be paid out during the April-to-December implementation period, with $2.4 million due upon final acceptance. That $9.6 million in-period funding fits within your $9 million current-year constraint plus some post-October funding, Leila — but I want to be precise here.

Before I record a decision, I need us to confirm: does the 20% holdback structure resolve the cash-flow timing issue so we can approve the full $12 million budget, or do we need to formally split the funding authorization between current year and post-October? I want to get this right before I sign off.

transcript.text: To answer your question directly, Maya, the 20% holdback helps but doesn't fully resolve the timing issue on its own. Let me lay out the numbers as I see them. With a 20% holdback on $12 million, $2.4 million is deferred until final acceptance, meaning $9.6 million would be payable during the April-to-December implementation period. My cash forecast shows only $9 million can be funded before the end of the current fiscal year while preserving the approved minimum cash floor, with the remaining $3 million available after October 1. So even with the holdback reducing in-period cash outflow to $9.6 million, that still exceeds my $9 million current-year funding capacity by $600,000. That $600,000 gap — plus the $2.4 million holdback due at final acceptance — would need to come from post-October funding. So my recommendation is that we formally split the funding authorization: $9 million within the current fiscal year and $3 million post-October 1, with the payment schedule structured so that no more than $9 million in invoices is actually paid out before the end of the fiscal year. The holdback gives us some flexibility on timing, but I wouldn't rely on it alone to bridge the gap without a formal split. Jonas, I'd also note that your capitalization split is relevant from my side too — the $4.8 million in period expense will hit cash differently than the $7.2 million capitalized portion, and I'll need to reflect that in my updated forecast before we finalize.
